And from the word *aluptaśakti*, [the mantra continues with] *padāt* and *netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*.
Then follows the word *sakhī* and *sakalaśatrupramardini*.
Then, with "Astrāya Phaṭ," one should complete the assignment of the limbs (aṅganyāsa);
thereafter, over the vessel of oblation (arghapātra), one should perform the rite with the mudrā known as Mīna.
Having recited the *ācchādanamūla* mantra ten times and performed the *amṛtīkaraṇa* (the rite of nectarization) with the *dhenu-mudrā*, one should sprinkle oneself with the waters.
Having protected the articles of worship with *ālābīja* mantras,
and having displayed the *bhūtinī*, *yoginī*, and *mudrās*, that water [should be used] again.
Having placed the sprinkling vessel, one should then sprinkle the articles of worship and oneself with that water using the root mantra.
Having drawn the yantra, one should thereafter perform the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā).
O twice-born one, listen as I describe the extraction of the yantra of Siddhilakṣmī.
One should draw a square with four doors, encircled by three circles,
and then draw an eight-spoked wheel, a sixteen-petaled lotus, and again an eight-petaled lotus.
One should contemplate a triangle in the center of a hexagon and within that, a bindu;
there, with undistracted mind, one should worship the goddess Siddhilakṣmī.
O great sage, I shall describe to you the yantra of the Mālā-mantra:
the seed-syllable of the Friend (Sakhībīja) is situated within a triangle, and outside of that, a hexagon is prescribed.
Then, one should draw the subterranean chamber (bhūgṛha), which has eight petals adorned with two seasonal petals, and which is threefold and possesses four corners.
I have described these two yantras of Siddhilakṣmī to you;
by seeing them one attains auspiciousness, and by touching them, one attains happiness.
Through salutation one attains liberation, and through worship one receives all accomplishments;
now I shall describe to you merely the construction of the yantra.
In a skull or a copper vessel made from the remains of a corpse,
on a Saturday or a Tuesday, O you who are born of Prajāpati!
A wheel should be fashioned from wood from a cremation ground, or from silver, gold, or even iron; listen to me regarding the attainment of the fortune of success (*siddhilakṣmī*).
73b) Now, O Brahmin, I shall describe their fruit in detail:
one attains happiness in the skull, both in this world and in the next.
In a copper vessel, there is auspiciousness; in a corpse, unsurpassed success;
in gold, there will be great happiness; and in silver, there is a great fruit.
If fashioned from the wood of a cremation ground, all accomplishments will certainly be attained;
if made of iron, there is devotion to the deity—thus, O twice-born one, has the fruit been described to you.
From here on, the wise practitioner should worship the successive deities of the *pīṭhas* as before;
thereafter, the seeker whose mind is intent on his desired goal should perform worship above that.
Having uttered the seed-syllable *medhī*, one should then recite the word *sadāśiva*;
thereafter, from the word *mahāpreta*, one should say "salutation to the lotus-throne" (*padmāsanāya namaḥ*).
O best of the twice-born, one should worship Narāsana and Mayūrāsana at that very place, and immediately thereafter, Mūṣakāsana.
Thereafter, having performed meditation as before,
the practitioner should bring forth a handful of flowers and then perform the invocation.
Having uttered the seed-syllable of the Friend (sakhībīja), that which is the word "Parāparā," followed by "Sūkṣmā" and "Khagasthā," and thereafter "Svasvarūpiṇi."
Then the Goddess went from the station of the world of the gods to that station;
having come from that station, she then took her place here in this mandala.
Having invoked [the deity] with this mantra, one should worship immediately thereafter;
then, after the seed-syllable of liberation (mokṣabīja), one should add "sakhī" and "prāntara-ścaṭyaḥ."
The seat of Jālandhara is proclaimed as the staff at the end;
then the seed-syllable of the female friend (sakhī), the intermediate space, and then the two *caṭa* seed-syllables.
The Pīṭha of Pūrṇagiri is "Nentaṃ daṇḍāntaṃ"; indeed, this is considered the mantra.
Likewise, the Pīṭha of Kāmarūpa consists of the "Sakhī," "Prāntara," and "Caṭī."
The wise one should worship the end of the staff with the fourth case-ending within the triangle;
thereafter, one should worship the Mistress of the Gods in the center of the bindu.
Then the *sakhī*, the desert (*prāntara*), the seed (*bīja*), and thereafter the *caṭībīja*;
[this is] the seat of the Great Preta (*mahāpreta*), ending with *na* and ending with the staff (*daṇḍa*), for the worship of the *bindu*.
O twice-born one, Śruti, Caṭīmāṇḍīra, and Ādyāta are intended;
O twice-born one, having again uttered Ādyāta, one should likewise perform the Daṇḍahoma and Homa.
Immediately after that, I worship the sandals of the Mother Goddess Śrīsiddhilakṣmī;
at the end [of the mantra], one performs worship with "namaḥ" in the center of the *bindu*.
Having meditated again upon the Great Goddess, the practitioner with a steady mind should recite the previously mentioned Gāyatrī and worship her once more in the center.
Having uttered "Śrutidaṇḍau," then "Sarvasiddhipadam," and having said "Yoginībhyaḥ," one should again recollect "Namaḥ."
Furthermore, salutation likewise to the Mothers, who are the state of all accomplishments;
to Nityoditā and Nanditā, the state of the entire wheel of the family.
Again, for the heroine and the Blessed Lady Caṇḍakāpālinī:
Śruti, Caṭīghārī, Juhu, Ādyā, and Daṇḍa.
From the state of the Supreme Swan (Paramahaṃsinī) comes the state that bestows the path to Nirvāṇa;
from the state of the Goddess (Devī) comes the state that pacifies the uneven [afflictions], and from that, the state of tranquility.
Then follows the word "pada" (the state), which crushes all evils, misfortunes, and afflictions,
and likewise the word "pada," which is a boat for crossing the ocean of all calamities.
Then the word "sakalaśatrupramathani," followed by "devi," and after that, the pair "āgaccha" and then the pair "hasa."
Having uttered "my enemies," he should say "crush" twice;
then he should say "eat" twice, "pierce with the trident" twice, and thereafter [say "kill"].
Having uttered the two syllables *chiṃdhi*, one should strike the two with a sword;
likewise, one should cut the two twice and strike the two twice as well.
Having uttered "all my desires," one should say "accomplish,
accomplish," and then the word for the Blessed One, who is supremely compassionate.
Then, O bearer of the form of Mahābhairava, supreme one,
saluted by the best of the thirty gods, and mother of all mantras!
O Goddess, who are affectionate toward those who bow before you, O destroyer of the Kali age!
[Grant] the seed-syllable of the Vedas, the three supports, and the very word "be gracious."
Having addressed her who is afflicted by passion, one should then utter the seed-syllable *caṭī*, followed by "do it twice," and then "the daughter of the gods and asuras" and again *caṭī*.
The prāntara, the seed-syllable of Gharī, the two *phaṭ*s, and the homa;
or else, I worship the pādukā of the goddess Śrīsiddhilakṣmī.
At the end of the *daṇḍa*, one should worship with the *aṅga-mantra* as taught by Manu;
now, O tiger among sages, hear from me the *bali-mantra*.
I worship the sandals of the Lord of the Ganas, the Seed of the Friend;
[saying] "Salutation," the wise one should offer an oblation to the west.

Then, one should worship the sandals of Kramavaṭukanātha, whose seed-syllable is *sakhī*; this is considered the mantra for the offering of the oblation (*bali*) to the infinite and all-pervading Lord.
In the southeast corner, the knower of mantras should worship with this mantra:
first the seed-syllable of the Friend (Sakhī), followed by the words "Kramavaṭukanāthavallabhā" (the beloved of Kramavaṭukanātha).
"I worship the Śrīpādukā; obeisance—thus it is concluded. In the southwest (Nairṛta) is the seed-syllable of the Friend (Sakhī) and the word Oṃ.
Thereafter, I worship the sandals of the Lord of the Pīṭha; immediately after that, at the end of "I worship" (pūjayāmi), one should again remember the Sakhī-bīja followed by "namaḥ."
Next, as before, offer the sandals to the Lord of Vṛṣasaṃketa;
then, in the northwest, place the seed-syllable of the female companion (sakhī) followed by the word "mahāphala."
Next, as before, offer the sandals to the Lord of the Heroic Cremation Ground (Vīraśmaśānanātha),
and thereafter the venerable sandals to the one who destroys all [the powers] of the female companion (Sakhī).
In the northeast (Īśāna), there is the seed-syllable of the female friend (sakhībīja), followed by the word "mahāsarva";
then follows the word for the Kṣetrapāla who is fierce with the power of withdrawal (saṃhāravalotkaṭa).
I worship the beloved sandals with the word "namaḥ.
Thereafter, in the center of the triangle, [one worships] with the words "nentaṃ haṃ sāsanā."
I worship the Śrīpādukā; at the end [of the mantra], the word "namaḥ" is added.
Likewise, [one worships] the bull, the peacock, Garuḍa, and the buffalo.
One should worship this lion until the end of the month with the [mantra] ending in "na. After this, one should place the eight Śaktis upon the eight petals.
Then the seed-syllable of the Friend (Sakhī), then the Goddess Brahmāṇī, her foot,
and thereafter the sandals together with Asitāṅga Bhairava.
One should worship those Śaktis with the mantra ending in "namas";
then [one worships] the goddess Sakhīmāheśvarī and the station of Rurubhairava.
Thereafter, the wise practitioner should worship the sandals together with the companions (sakhīs), beginning from the east;
then the goddess Kaumārī and the station of Caṇḍabhairava.
The goddess Vaiṣṇavī is the companion of Krodhabhairava,
and the goddess Vārāhī is the companion of Unmattabhairava.
That very seed-syllable belongs to the goddess Indrāṇī; hear it from me next:
the word "Kāpālīśabhairava," followed by the words beginning with "sahitā."
Then [one should worship] the goddess Cāmuṇḍā, the terrifying state, and the Bhairava state;
indeed, at the end of the sandals (pādukā), she is accompanied everywhere by all her companions.
I worship the feet of the goddess Mahālakṣmī, the companion of Saṃhārabhairava, together with her sandals; thereafter, I offer salutations.
With this mantra, one should offer them an oblation at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice;
having performed worship on the eight petals, one should then worship on the solar petal.
Having first established the seed-syllable of the companion (sakhībīja) everywhere, the practitioner,
having placed the sandals upon his feet, performs worship and offers salutations.
One should worship all the female companions (sakhīs) at the beginning and end of the rite as impelled by the sequence;
likewise, having worshipped Śivā within the Goddess, one should worship the divine Bhagavatī.
The best of practitioners should know that the word "ca" or "vā" occurs at the end of the name of the Goddess; following that are the names Māyādevī, Bhadrādevī, and Ki[rti]devī.
After that is Queen Vimalā, then the goddess Yamajihvā;
after her is Queen Ghaṭodarī; listen further, O twice-born one.
Then one should utter the two syllables following "cauramātari-devīm.
Then, having offered a footstep to the Goddess, one should worship her feet as before.
Thereafter, one should always worship the goddess Kākinī as before;
likewise, one should offer the bali offering and then worship in the eight-cornered [mandala].
Having uttered the *śruti* mantra at the seed-syllable of Caṭī, one should worship the eight female leaders (*nāyikā*),
addressing Ugracaṇḍā preceded by those two seed-syllables.
Having offered [the oblations] from Ambā up to the sandals (pādukā) to the Supreme One, the wise practitioner should worship Ugracaṇḍa,
Caṇḍa, Caṇḍogrā, and Caṇḍanāyikā.
To Caṇḍā, Caṇḍavatī, Caṇḍarūpā, and Caṇḍikā,
one should offer an oblation as before and worship as before.
Thereafter, O Brahmin, the foremost of practitioners should worship the seed-syllable of the Sakhī,
namely *Ḍāṃ*, followed by "Ḍākinīmbā Pādukām" within the hexagon.
O Nārada, one should worship everything in this manner, starting from the east and so forth:
RĀṂ to Rākinī, LĀṂ to Lākinī, and thereafter KĀṂ to Kākinī.
Having worshipped that Sākinī, O twice-born one, one should thereafter worship Hākinī; as before, one should offer the great bali and perform the worship as previously described.
Furthermore, one should worship in the center; hear that mantra, O Nārada:
the word *sakhī*, followed by *prāntaracaṭya*, and after that, the seed-syllable of liberation (*mokṣabīja*).
O Brahmin, with this mantra, one should cause an offering of bali to be presented for the sake of the Oḍiyāna seat, including both the sandals and the footprint itself.
O best of the twice-born, the female parrot dwelling in the midst of the friend is the seed-syllable of liberation;
from that very source indeed comes the sandals for the Jālandhara seat.
76a) O son of Brahmā, listen to this second mantra for the *vali* [offering]:
first the seed-syllable of the female friend (*sakhī*), then the intermediate one, and likewise the supreme seed-syllable of the female crow (*caṭī*).
O twice-born one, the sandals for the seat of Kāmarūpa are [offered] as before;
this mantra is proclaimed for the third offering of the bali.
One should worship the great goddess Siddhilakṣmī with ritual offerings;
now I shall speak the words for the gift, listen, O Nārada.
One should utter the formula ending with "daṇḍa" when offering water for the feet (pādya), that ending with "homa" when offering the respectful oblation (arghya),
and likewise that ending with "svadhā" when offering water for sipping (ācamanīya) and so forth.
First, having uttered the root [mantra], the wise one should then say "it should be given" (deya);
at the end of that, he should state the recipient (saṃpradāna), and then the word signifying renunciation (tyāga).
O Nārada, one should perform the ritual services (upacāras) in due order;
then, one should present those services with their respective mantras.
Then, having recited the Sāvitrī mantra and the root mantra with the secret rosary,
and having performed the recitation according to one's capacity, one should offer it with the "Guhyātiguhyam" verse and others.
Thereafter, the foremost of practitioners, bowing with this hymn of praise, said:
"O Goddess, you are Viṣṇu’s Māyā, the supreme Pārvatī consisting of primordial nature."

And you are Svāhā, the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution; you are composed of all virtues, the agent, and the sustainer. You are the sole essence of the world, the remover of fear for those who bow to you, and merged upon the supreme head of Śaṅkara. I bow to her who has ten arms white with conchs and moon-like earrings, and who possesses five faces.
Thereafter, the wise one, having bowed down and drawn the floral remains from the seat by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*,
should place them upon the ground-maṇḍala in the northeast.
Then, having fashioned a triangle, one should worship Nirmālyavāsinī;
having gratified Nirmālyavāsinī, one should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*).
Thereafter, O wise one, the intelligent practitioner should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and the breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma).
Furthermore, O Nārada, he should accept some of the water from the feet (pādodaka) and the remains of the offerings (nirmālya).
"O Nārada, having spoken thus, those [deities] performed the perpetual worship for the sake of the Goddess of Siddhi."
Now, O twice-born one, tell me indeed what you wish to hear.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Daily Worship," in the *Śrī Kālānala Tantra* concerning Nailalohita.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, Lord of Compassion, Ocean of Mercy, Nīlalohita!
By your grace, I have heard everything concerning the fortune of perfection in its entirety.
"Regarding those services that were described by you before me in the ritual of worship, Śrī Nīlalohita said:
'Excellent, O Nārada! You are blessed; your mind has spoken rightly.'"
For it is certain that accomplishment arises as a consequence.
I shall explain it in detail; listen with an attentive mind, O best of Brahmins, for I am always pleased with you.
I shall describe the ritual services; listen to them, O twice-born one:
the seat, welcome, water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and water for sipping (ācamanīya).
Bathing, clothing, and sacred threads, as well as ornaments of every kind;
likewise, perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, food, and a mirror.
With garlands and ointments, as well as prostrations and dismissal,
the mantra-practitioner should perform the worship consisting of the eighteen services.
O twice-born one, in their absence, the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra) should be offered:
water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), bathing (snāna), garments, and ornaments.
Then [offer] perfumes and flowers, incense and lamps, food offerings and water for sipping; thereafter, betel, worship, hymns of praise, libations, and prostrations.
One should employ the sixteen modes of service (upacāra) in the place of worship;
O Nārada, in their absence, ten modes of service should be performed.

Water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), as well as food (anna), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), water for sipping (ācamana), as well as perfumes (gandha) and so forth, ending with the food offering (naivedya)— these are to be known as the ten ritual services (daśopacāra).
O twice-born one, the worship with five offerings (pañcopacāra-pūjā) should be performed with diligence;
the fivefold worship consists of offerings beginning with fragrance and ending with food (naivedya).
O Lotus-born one, I shall now declare to you the mantra for giving;
O Nārada, a separate mantra has been prescribed for every ritual act.
Listen as I speak briefly regarding the gift of clothing:
one should recite the mantra for each pair of garments, such as those made of cotton or silk, in pairs.
Then, having uttered "Siddhilakṣmī," one should remember the two [mantras] for taking the garment;
*tāla* and *haum* are to be known as supreme, while the *vaṭa* mantra is for the offering of the garment.
Henceforth, learn from me the mantra for collyrium (kajjala).
Having remembered the Śruti and the Yuga, one should recite it during a most terrible time.
Then one should utter the pair *hini*, *kajjapa*, and the two *gṛh* syllables;
this mantra for the offering of collyrium is proclaimed to end with the oblation (*homānta*).
Thereafter, O beloved, one should apply vermilion with this mantra:
"Khecarī, Bhūcarī, Ṛkṣā, Kālasī, and likewise Kulaṭā."
Prattāṅgī, Dhībalī, Śvetā, Kirāṭī, and Varaṭā—
O Goddess mounted upon a white corpse, thereafter the state of Siddhilakṣmī.
Having said "my enemy," one should utter "paralyze" (staṃbhaya);
having spoken the pair [of syllables] "destroy" (vidhvaṃsaya), one should then recollect "from the planets" (grahebhyaḥ).
"Bestow peace! Bestow protection! [Then] the supreme and non-supreme peak-syllable. This mantra, ending with *phaṭ*, is declared to be for the application of vermilion (*siṃdūra*).
O son of Brahmā, hear from me this mantra for the offering of the seat: *saṃbhava*, followed by *varuḍī*, *gāruḍī*, or *bhagavatī*. Then the word *pada*.
Then, having uttered "Siddhilakṣmī" and "Upaveśaya," one should say "Yugam.
O best of the twice-born, this mantra, ending with "svāhā," is to be known for the offering of the seat (*pīṭhārpaṇa*).
Listen quickly and with diligence to my mantra for the application of lac-dye:
having first uttered the pair *retasaḥ*, one should then recite the phrase *navakoṭi*.
Then, after "yoginī," followed by "na" and ending with "ntaṃ," thus surrounded;
this mantra is to be known, O twice-born one, for the offering of lac at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa).
O Brahmin, listen now to this mantra for the offering of incense, O twice-born one:
*Dhruvā, Dhuvācī, Dhamanī, Dhayantī, and likewise Dhāraṇī.*
Having said, "This incense," one should utter the nose-mantra and the pair [of hands].
Now hear the procedure for the offering of incense according to the mantra of Agni’s consort.
Now, understand from this point forward the Dīpamanu of Siddhilakṣmī:
it is changeless, supportless, and effortless.
Then one should utter "Timirāśamidaṃ dīpaṃ gṛhṇa yugmaṃ," followed by the Māheśvara kūṭa and ending with "phaṭ"; this is considered the mantra.
Now listen, O dear son of Nārada, to the mantra for the offering of fragrance:
Dardurī, Durmadā, Ādīrghā, Dogdhrī, Dolā, and Vihangamī.
"Oṃ gandhārpaṇam anu svāhā; receive, receive, O ender of the oblation!"—O best of the twice-born, listen now to the mantra for the offering of flowers here.
And then, in sequence, a pair of pairs of bees for the ears and the voice;
I offer this flower to the Goddess of Accomplishment (Siddhilakṣmī) thereafter.
Nihrādinī, Paliknī, Madhukā, Citrinī, Pretārūḍhā, Siddhilakṣmī, Chatra, and then this Pada.
And with devotion, I offer you the presentation of the parasol;
a wise man should recite this for each pair of "milkers of the Vedas" and "semen."
Then, O Blessed One Siddhilakṣmī, one should eat two morsels;
having consumed two mouthfuls, one should perform the desired tāla and homa rites.
O twice-born one, this Manu has been described to you regarding the rite of offering food;
now listen as I explain to you this procedure for the offering of the conch.
The flocks resounded with the cries of female ospreys, as did the cranes and the *veśmarī* birds;
"Take this pure conch, take it!"—this mantra ends with *svāhā*.
O twice-born one, I shall now describe the granting of the general ornaments:
the Haṃsakūṭa, the Vyomakūṭa, the Cāmara, the Haima, and the Indu.
"O Siddhilakṣmī, accept this such-and-such ornament; *namaḥ svāhā*. This is declared to be the mantra for the rite of bestowing ornaments.
I shall declare the penance for giving unmentioned substances; listen to me.
[The penances are] Śruti, Caṭī, Vāṇī, Retaḥ, Paśu, and a pair of Yugas.
Having uttered "O Goddess Siddhilakṣmī, accept this," the practitioner [should say]:
"I offer such-and-such a substance; please accept the pair, svāhā!"
O twice-born one, Manu has already described to you the gift of common substances;
now listen as I describe to you the supreme place for the gift of wealth.
O twice-born one, one should place the perfume, flowers, and ornaments directly in front;
the lamp should be offered on the right, and likewise the incense on the left.
One should offer whatever food is cooked as the sacrificial oblation (naivedya) in the southern region, and that which is uncooked on the left side; now hear further concerning the lamp.
One should offer a lamp filled with ghee, having seven wicks or even more,
on the right side, while the other [lamp] should be placed on the left side.
O Nārada, the practitioner should offer pure fragrance with the tips of the middle, ring, and thumb fingers, while reciting the root mantra.
O Brahmin, as with the incense, so should the wise man offer it;
the preceptor should do so using the middle and ring fingers at the middle joints.
O Brahman-sage, holding the incense with the tip of the thumb, one should offer it;
having divided that weight into three parts, [one should do so] with the Gāyatrī and the root mantra.
O Brahmin, one should present the food offering with the mudrā called Tattva;
one should offer the water for sipping (ācamana) with the root mantra, and the betel leaf with the Tattva-mudrā.
Neither a flower nor a leaf is desired if held with its face downward;
one should not ring a bell that has not been worshipped, and one should burn guggulu incense.
Now listen, O brahmin-sage, to my description of incense:
guggulu, śarala, dārupatra, and that which originates from Malaya.
Hrīvera, aguru, kuṣṭha, jaggery, sarjarasa,
ghanasāra, harītakī, nakhī, lākṣā, jaṭāmāṃsī, and śailaja.
They know that incense for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors consists of sixteen ingredients:
honey, sugar, clarified butter, fragrance, guggulu, and śailaja (bdellium).
Śarala, sihlaka, and siddhārtha are said to constitute the ten-ingredient incense (daśāṅgadhūpa),
along with guggulu, aguru, and candana, mixed with sugar, clarified butter, and honey.
That six-ingredient incense is always dear to all the gods;
it consists of guggulu, aguru, uśīra, sugar, honey, and sandalwood.
"The preceptor should burn incense mixed with clarified butter below the deity.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have related this answer to your question to you.
What shall I speak of now? Tell me that, O Nārada.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual Services," in the *Śrī Kālānala Tantra* concerning Nailalohita.
Śrī Nārada said:
O Nīlalohita, O Lord, O increaser of the joy of Girijā!
By your grace, I have heard everything regarding the worship of Siddhilakṣmī.
79a) And tell me of the author of the *Rahasyamālā* and the state of being Nīlalohita; for whom would each garland be intended, and for whom do these garlands grant the fruits of desire?

beyond that, O deluder of Sadāśiva, the supreme one who transcends the qualities (guṇātīta).

"O you who give rise to pure being, the quality of goodness, consciousness, and bliss."
*Dogdhrī*, *tālam*, *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, and the *praṇava* (Oṃ), then *caṭī*;
*samīhā*, *śoṣiṇī*, *śiraḥ*, *dolā*, *aṅkuśa*, and the two *jaya*s.
After the word *mahānāgarājabhūṣitapadāt* comes the pair of *jīva*s;
then the word *daśabhujadaṇḍe*, and also *caṇḍacaṇḍātitara*.
From that point, the word *karavāravinikṛttasakala* [is used] as an address (*saṃbodhana*) directed toward the fragments of the bodies of the Daityas and Dānavas.

Sasaṃha, Śoṣiṇī, Śiva, Dolā, Aṅkuśa, and the two Jayas;
then the two Jīvas, the mind, the sense objects, and thereafter the sphere of passion.
Then, upon the supreme body composed of the three qualities (triguṇa),
there was a tiger-skin garment and likewise a height of eight palm trees (samīhātāla).
The staff-offering (daṇḍahoma), the two ears of the Veda (śruticaṭī), the milch-cow (dogdhrī), as well as the emaciated woman (śoṣiṇī),

Then, although he was radiant with a mass of wildly swaying matted locks,
he was as cool and soft as snow, jasmine, the moon, camphor, and the essence of the *kambu* flower.
Then, for the purpose of severing the bonds of old age, birth, and saṃsāra, there are the Dogdhrī,
the Tāla-daṇḍa-homa, as well as the Tāra, Māyā, and Krodha.
Śoṣiṇī, Śirasī, Dolā, Sṛṇi,
Jayadvaya, Jīvadvaya, Viprarṣi, Guhya, and Atiparama.
Then, [it is] secret, hidden within the reality of the supreme and lower Śiva-śakti;
then, it is the experience of bliss, established in the state of self-luminosity.
That supreme state is merged upon the couch of the play of *sāmarasya* (cosmic harmony);
likewise, there are the *dogdhrī*, *tāla*, *daṇḍahoma*, as well as *tāra*, *māyā*, and *krodha*.
She is the withering one, the swing of the head, the goad, and the pair of Victories;
she is the pair of lives, transcending both Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
O witness of the highest good, O protectress of the three worlds, O devourer of Daityas and Dānavas!
O yielder of desires, O staff, O oblation, and likewise the beginning of the Vedas, O Catī!
The pair of Victors, who withers desire, whose head is the goad of the swing,
who are the two lives, and who set in motion the entire wheel of the Kaula doctrine.
O Goddess who causes fear to all the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas;
O Goddess Sudhā, arisen from the Ocean of Milk, you are superior even to the supreme state.
O you who drink the essence of excellence, who reside within the belly of the three worlds,
who cause the bondage of those possessing only the quality of goodness (sattva), O illusory one!
Then one should say, "There will be great pestilence, foreign invasion, and famine," and thereafter,
"Great portents and the dissolution of the world."
One should then recite: "Dogdhri-tālam, Daṇḍī-homa, Tāra-vaṃtra-pākrodhau, as well as the pair of Jayas and the pair of Jīvas—thus it is 'vividha'."
Then, O bird of the cage consisting of the mantras of the six traditions, grant me that state which has reached the further shore of the application of divine weapons.
O Goddess who has made all bodies her ornaments! O you who possess eight serpents!
O giver of milk! O you who hold the staff and the sacrificial ladle! O you who are high-pitched, modest, and wrathful!
One should declare Śoṣiṇī, Śirasī, Dolā, Aṅkuśā, the two Jayās,
the two Jīvās, and Niṣkalā as transcending the phenomenal world (prapañca).
Then, O Sage Nārada, listen to that which is of the nature of the Fourth (Turya), which is the supreme undivided bliss, and which is the flow of the nectar of self-knowledge.
O Nārada, in the essence of the truth of the Nigamas and Āgamas, there are Dogdhrītāla,
Daṇḍahoma, Śruti, Caṭīdogdhrī, and likewise Śoṣiṇī.
The head, the swing, the goad, and the pair "jaya-jīva"—
these two bestow the eightfold supernatural powers (siddhis), beginning with Mahākhecarī.
Dogdhri, tāla, daṇḍahoma, śruti, caṭī,
as well as samīhā, śoṣiṇī, śiras, dolā, aṅkuśa, and the two jayas.
O you whose lotus feet are to be worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
O you whose neck is adorned with a garland of human skulls—this is the word of address.
O great sage, thereafter, having brought all the gods and asuras together in a great assembly,
[one should utter] "Dhoktrī-tālam namaḥ svāhā" twice for the sake of victory.
In the Satya Yuga, the pair of victories known as Pratyamgira and Jayat is remembered;
in the Tretā Yuga, it is Siddhilakṣmī and Jayat; and beyond that [in the Dvāpara], it is likewise.
In the Dvāpara age, O Royal Fortune, the pair of Jayas is remembered as supreme;
and in the Kali age, O fierce Kāpālinī, that very same [pair] is supreme.
Then one should say "śrutivāṇī," "valadā," "medhinakrau," and thereafter,
following the word "bhagavati," one should utter the pair "padāccaiva prasīda."
Then follow a pair of *jvala*, a pair of *prajvala*, a pair of *sphura*,
and thereafter a pair of *prasphura*, as well as a pair of *caṭa*.
There is also the pair of recitation, the pair of singing, the pair of dancing, and the pair of storytelling; what [is] the pair beyond that?
Tvaradhāva-yugam, yugam, dogdhrī, śivaḥ, tathā,
dolāṅkuśam, caṭī, and then the word vyomakeśi-padam.
Vidyutkeśi piṅgakeśi phaṭ svāhā huṃ, followed by that;
then Śiro-dolāṅkuśa-caṭyau bhagamālini, following that.
Then, at the *bhaga-prade* [syllable], there are *bhaga-priye*, *tāla-homa*, and *dogdhrī*;
then, at the *madanonmādini* [syllable], there are *śirodolā*, *aṅkuśa*, and *caṭī*.
O you who devour the flesh of corpses, O you who converse with Brahmā!
Then: *phaṭ svāhā hūṃ*, as well as the head, the swing, the goad, and *caṭī*.
There is a single word for the ornament of a garland of hell-wardens,
and there is likewise a single word for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra.
Then: *tribhuvananandinacaraṇe phaṭ svāhā*. Next: *dogdhrī*, *śiro*, *dolāṅkuśa*, *caṭī*, and *vamadagnimukhi*.
Then, O Great Sage, when he was surrounded by tens of millions upon tens of millions of jackals, and when the three worlds were terrified by the clapping of his hands;
At the time of the great dissolution, she danced with her limbs outstretched;
thereafter, she caused the seven continents to revolve by the striking of her feet.
The palm tree, the fire-oblation, the caṭī-dogdhrī, the head, the swing, and the goad;
likewise, the placement of the feet of the caṭī, followed by the bending of the foot.
And upon the body of the serpent Śeṣa, who is like a tortoise, following the vocative address,
[he is seated] upon the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) of all beings.
The reality within the scope of the Nigamas, Agamas, Itihasas, and Puranas;
likewise, the syllables *phaṭ*, *svāhā*, *huṃ*, *preṃ*, the swing (*dolā*), the hook (*aṅkuśa*), and *caṭī*.
The word "jaṅgama" (the moving one) refers to that which removes the mental anguish of devotees and is born from that which has transcended the three types of suffering. It is also called "jaṅgama."
"Then [the name] 'Savior of All Beings,' and immediately after that,
'Illuminator of the Lotus-heart of the God of Gods.'"
O Brahmin, having thus accomplished the *siddhi* within the single orb of the sun,
there arose the *tāla-homa*, the *śruti*, the *vāṇī*, and likewise the ground of the *caṭī-siddhi*.
The emission of semen provides pleasure; immediately thereafter follows the swing that dries up the seminal flow, as well as the goad and the crest of the head, along with the female companion.
[He is the master] of all the daityas, dānavas, asuras, yakṣas, and rākṣasas;
likewise of the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, kuṣmāṇḍas, and ḍākinīs.
Then there are the words for *śākinī*, as well as *skanda* and *vināyaka*;
likewise the words for *dyoṇaka*, *kṣetrapāla*, and *vetāla*.
One should likewise speak of the state of *brahmarākṣasa*, *guhya*, and *gandharva*, as well as of serpents, *nāgas*, planets, lunar mansions, spirits, and insanity.
Then there are the three kinds of portents: thieves, fire, and wild beasts or predators;
as well as war, thunderbolts, destruction, clouds, lightning, and earthquakes.
Then [there follow] rain, poison, secondary poisons, sorcery, and malevolent rites;
thereafter, deception, fraud, famine, and the destruction of cities.
Next are the words for causing calamity to a region, paralyzing, and deluding; following that are the words for subjugation, inciting hatred, and expulsion.
Then [he sees] the Veśana river, the whirlpools, and the places;
as well as the desert, the wind, fire, worms, insects, and winged creatures.
From the footprints of land-dwellers and water-dwellers, there then follows the footprint of the porcupine;
and likewise those of two-footed, four-footed, six-footed, and eight-footed beings.
One should then recollect that which consists of many syllables and is formidable, beginning with the syllable *dhakāra*,
followed by the words *mahāmārī-vāla-graha-hiṃsaka-sarva*.
One should know that the word *māyā* refers to that which steals one's sleep and is intent on deceiving people;
furthermore, words such as *devila*, *dasyu*, and *vañcaka* follow from that [same root].
Then [the mantra] for the night-wanderers and those active at twilight: *śṛṅgi svapadam*.
Then for the fanged ones and various calamities: *mām*. Then from [the word] *bhyaḥ*.
Then, having uttered the pair "rakṣa," the pair "pāhi," the pair "pālaya," and then the pair "samuddhara," [one should utter] the two "abhaya" [mantras].
O Nārada, thereafter [worship] Prasīda and Anukampā;
then Śatruhā and Unmūlā.
Chindi chindi, O Great Sage, [then] yugaṃ yugaṃ, māraya yugalama, tataḥ nāśaya yugalama, and also hanad dvayam.
Then, the pair "uccāṭaya" (expel), the pair "staṃbhaya" (paralyze),
the pair "matha" (churn), and the pair "vidhvaṃśaya" (destroy) are proclaimed.
Purify the pair of *truṭis*; cause [them] to flee in pairs;
terrify the two; delude the two; then cause the two to flee.
The pair "sphoṭaya," the pair "jṛmbhaya," likewise the pair "haraya," the pair "vikṣobhaya," and then the pair "mardaya."
The pair *dama*, the pair *turu*, the pair *hili*, the two *kini*s,
the pair *hana*, the pair *bhakṣaya*, and then the pair *kṛntaya*.
He likewise crushed the pair of Vipras and the pair of Piṣas;
he also stole the pair of Coras and similarly broke the pair of Bhas.
Reduce both to ashes, likewise draw both toward you;
cause the pair to fall, cause the pair to tremble, and then cause the pair to be agitated.
And also the pair beginning with *āveśaya*, likewise the pair beginning with *unmādaya*;
O God, the pair beginning with *om maya*, and then the pair beginning with *lunīhi*.
Then, after that, one should utter the pair "āskandaya," the pair "muñca," the pair "luñca," the pair "piva," as well as "jāraya" and "sthā."
In her own skull-cup is the seed-syllable *vlauṃ*, and likewise *bhagavati glauṃ*;
likewise *mahāpracaṇḍini* and the syllable *kṣauṃ* for *vidāriṇī*.
Then Trīṃ, Muṇḍamālini, Carvāka,
immediately after that Mahāgrāsa, and then Mālatībīja.
Following that, the seed-syllable released from the feet of Pārvatī;
after that, the seed-syllable of Mahābhūti, and then likewise the Sannaddha seed-syllable.
Then [follow] *bhujaṅga* and *kiṅkiṇī*, and after that the seed-syllable of *kavaṇdha*;
then *pātālavāsini*, and finally *navabījāntacāriṇi*.
Kokamukhi, Dogdhrī, Bīja, Raktatuṇḍi, and after that Dogdhrī; Rudrādhārā and then Dogdhrī, and thereafter Ṛkṣakarṇī.
Huṃ, Jāri; thereafter, Tadanuvidyuddhāse;
thereafter, Huṃ, Candrabhāle; thereafter, Śavari.
Having addressed the Kirāta-foot, [one says]: "Huṃ! O you who devour corpses! Huṃ!
O you who delight in the ocean of milk! Huṃ! O you who crave the state of essential identity!"
Huṃ! O you who wander upon Kailāsa! Huṃ! O wish-fulfilling creeper for devotees! Huṃ! O bestower of desires! Huṃ! O you who bring about the eightfold supernatural powers!
Huṃ! O bestower of sovereignty and royal power, O Queen of the Kings of Kings! Huṃ! O you with lightning-like side-glances! Huṃ! O you who are immersed in the ocean of nectar!
Huṃ! O Maṇidharīvajriṇī, huṃ! O you whose state is that of Mahāḍāmarī! Huṃ! In fulfilling service with devotion, hūṃ! O bestower of the fruits of the four aims of life!
Then the seed-syllable *dogdhri*, then the *tāra* (om), then the word *muktipadam* in the sense of non-duality (*advaita*),

"Grant me the attainment of perfection, svāhā! O Tāra, the state beyond the fourth!
Reveal your own state, svāhā! Then, O Great Sage, [the syllable] Tāra!"
Therefore, bestow upon me knowledge in that which is the very nature of consciousness and bliss, svāhā!
Oṃ, and manifest yoga in that which is the very nature of sound and the point, svāhā!
Oṃ! O you whose form consists of consciousness, bestow omniscience upon me;
and likewise, bestow the state of perfection upon this body composed of the mantras of the fire-oblation and the Vedas.
Contemplate the state of equilibrium between Śiva and Śakti, Svāhā!
Oṃ, O lamp-flame of knowledge, [dispel] the darkness of ignorance from the state.
90a) Then [utter] *apanaya*, then *svāhā*, and after that *vedaśiras*; then [utter] *sarvavidyāmaya* consisting of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahma*).
Then, O Nārada, establish the seed-syllable *svāhā* and the seed-syllable of the Vedas (*śruti-bīja*);
thereafter, [place] this word which has the form of the forest fire of worldly existence (*saṃsāra-dāvāgni*).
Remove birth and death, svāhā! Oṃ, O you who are compassionate toward devotees! Pacify my miserable state, svāhā! And Tāra, O Nārada!
O You whose nature is the three Vedas, likewise, deliver me from sin, Svāhā!
Oṃ, bestow devotion upon me toward the state of You, the Inner Controller of all.
First is the *tāra* (the syllable Om) for the fire-oblation; then [the mantra] "O you who know all intentions";
then the oblation likewise with the words "Unite me with the three aims of life" (*trivarga*).
Oṃ, O you whose face is gracious, please me with excellent forms, svāhā!
Oṃ, O lioness of the Vedas, Agamas, and Forests, [bestow] upon me thereafter [the state of] selflessness.
"Haṃtāmapanuda svāhā," then the nine-syllable *tāra*,
and then, O Sage, hear the phrase for the consecration (*adhivāsa*) performed with the mantra.
"Deliver us all from danger, svāhā! After that, Tāraṃ;
O destroyer of all calamities, grant us all well-being."
Then the two *kuru*s, followed by *svāhā*, the *tāra* (oṃ), and *valadā*;
then *retomedhi*, *nakra*, and the word *sūryāsane*.
Having uttered the word *pada* in the form of *prabhā*, then *daṇḍa* and *tāla* for you;
then *tāla*, *valadā*, *retomedhi*, and *nakraka*.
Then, on the moon-seat (candrāsana) to the west, there is the word "candrikārūpe," followed by "taṇḍa," "tāla," "śruti," and "valadāre."
Then, having uttered "medhirn nakaḥ" at the seat of the purifier (pāvakāsane),
one should likewise utter the word for the flame-form (jvālārūpe) and "tubhyaṃ daṇḍītālaṃ."
90b) Valadā and Caireto, then Medhi, and beyond that the seed-syllable of Nakra; this is the seat of Hiraṇyagarbha, O Great Sage.
Having uttered the word "sṛṣṭirūpe," [one says] "namaḥ" for you, and likewise "phaṭ.
Then follow "vedaśivaḥ," "valadāre," and "to medhiḥ" thereafter.

O crocodile, from you who abide in the form of the seat of Nārāyaṇa, there arises the movement of the rhythmic beats and the flowing of the musical intervals; thus, the sacrificial post and the crocodile emerge.
Then follows the word of invocation upon the great Bhairava-seat:
"Obeisance to you in the form of dissolution," and after that, the syllable *phaṭ*.
After that, the Valadāreta, the Medhinakra, and the Vedāsana;
then the Gāyatrī-form, the Śruti, and the Daṇḍa itself.
Tāla, tāra, valā, retas, medhī, and nakraka;
for you, who are the sacrificial seat and the form of the oblation, there is the staff and the palm-leaf fan.
Salutations to you, who are the Śruti, the Valadāreta, the Medhi, and likewise the Nakra; salutations to you, who are the Ācāra, the Āsana, and that which conforms to Dharma.
Salutations again to you, whose form is rain upon the seat of Parjanya, and who are Tāla, Tāra, Valada, Śukramedhī, and Nakraka.
O you who are the hearing of weapons, the giver of strength, the sacrificial post, and the crocodile; salutations to you, the seat of food, whose form is the vital breath, and whose word is *phaṭ*.
O you whose power is the strength of the Vedas, O destroyer of the wicked, thereafter [is] Maṃtrāsana; obeisance to you in the form of initiation, Phaṭ!
Obeisance to you who are Śruti, Valadā, Reta, Medhi, and Nakra; obeisance to you whose seat is the vow and whose form is austerity, and obeisance to Phaṭ.
91a) Then, on the seat of the stars, the wise one should likewise be situated in the Nakra (Capricorn);
then on the seat of Ananta, and then the foot in the form of the Earth.
For you, O Nārada, there are Daṇḍī, Tāla, Tāra, and likewise Valadā; Medhī, Nakra, Nirākāra, Āsana, and indeed Pada.
To you, whose form is space, one should then utter "daṇḍītālaṃ tāraṃ";
thereafter, "valadāreto medhinakrāstribhuvanāsane."
Obeisance to you, whose form is all-powerful; likewise, [obeisance] to Daṇḍītāla, Śrutivala, Dāretha, Soma, Edhinakra, and Nārada.
Salutation to you, who are upon the seat of all sentient beings in the form of activity, *namaśca phaṭ*;
from that very source, the wise ones are struck by the force of the power of hearing.
Then, [I offer] obeisance to you in the form of yoga upon the seat of the *mūlādhāra*; thereafter, [I offer] obeisance to you as *tāla*, *tāra*, and likewise *valadā*.
Śukra, Medhī, and Kuṃbhīra; thereafter, upon the Brahmā-seat:
"Salutation to you who are eternally risen in the form of bliss, and likewise Phaṭ."
The syllables *vā*, *ṇī*, *lū*, *tā*, *vi*, *haṃ*, *saṃ*, *pā*, *dā*, *trī*, and thereafter *ta*;
then *ri*, *duḥ*, *ṣi*, *ta*, *rai*, *varṇyai*, and the seed-syllable of *veśmarī*.
The Asura and Vāgbhava, as well as the pair of engagement and withdrawal;
thereafter, she is the one who sets in motion the two paths, and that which is beyond them.
Since the Vedas and other scriptures manifest two forms,
how then can the Vedic tradition subsequently be the means of knowing that [reality] which transcends sound?
"Vrūvaḥ ste mahimānam," "tvam asi pratyaṅgirā," then "tataḥ," "śivā ca ḍākinī caiva," and after that, "svam asi."
Then you are Caṇḍakāpālinī, and after that Śivā; next you are Ḍākinī, and following that, you are Asiguhyakālī as well as Ḍākinī.

O Sage, you are Kāmakalākālī; therefore, you are that pair of seed-syllables. You are Tripurasundarī, the auspicious Ḍākinī; therefore, you are indeed Rājamātaṅgī, for you are that very same pair of seed-syllables.
You are Kuvjikā, and likewise the pair of Vījas, O Sage;
you are Harasiddhā, and beyond that, Śivā-Ḍākinī.
You are the seed-syllable of Vālā; listen well to those two. You are the seed-syllable of Tārā, and you are Bhairavī as well.
O Sage, you are the seed-syllable of Cāmuṇḍā; you are Chinnamastā, and you are the seed-syllable of Ugracaṇḍā.
You are Caṇḍīśvarī in your seed-syllable; you are Bhuvaneśvarī in that seed-syllable;
and you are Mahiṣamardinī in those two seed-syllables.
You are Vāgīśvarī, O Lord of Sages, and those two syllables are your seed-mantras;
you are Śivadūtī, and those two syllables are likewise your seed-mantras.

You are Mahālakṣmī, and you are the seed-syllable (bīja) of that; you are the word (pada), and you are the seed-syllable of the word "Rājarājeśvarī" (Queen of the Kings of Kings). Therefore, you are [all these].
Then you were the seed-syllable of Svarṇakūṭeśvarī;
then, O Sage, you were the seed-syllable of Jaya-jhaṅkeśvarī.
The Uchiṣṭacāṇḍālī mantra, followed by those two seed-syllables (bījas), is indeed that very same [mantra];
you are Kālarātri, and [your mantra] consists of those same two seed-syllables.
You are the bringer of peace, the auspicious Ḍākinī, and beyond that;
you are Vābhravī, whose seed-syllable is *te*, and from that you are.
92a) Following that, you are Raktadantikā in her seed-syllable;
furthermore, you are Aparājitā in her seed-syllable, as well as Vāṇīśruti and Prabaṃdhaka.
The *haṃsa* and the *mahāvākya* are also [means] for that which consists of cessation (*nivṛtti*);
beyond that, however, the nature [of reality] is impossible to describe, and only the *Śruti* [can testify to it].
"O bull among sages, listen: she is bodiless and devoid of sense organs;
she is without form, taste, smell, touch, or sound. Then he should speak thus.
Then, O Nārada, you shall attain that state which is the non-duality of "That" and "Thou," free from birth and death, and devoid of speech, hands, anus, and genitals.
After [teaching] that which transcends speech, taking, going, excretion, and sexual intercourse,
and having uttered the words "That thou art," the Śruti thereafter [reveals] the lake of the heart.
Then follows the three-syllabled [mantra] pervading the three times; immediately after that, the pair of Vedic verses beginning with "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) is traditionally remembered.
It is unattainable by the mind or speech, devoid of name and form,
the very state of "That thou art," and thus, according to the Vedas, it is changeless.
She is stainless, effortless, unattached, and beyond the qualities;
she is the two Vedic statements "That thou art" and likewise the eternal state.
Therefore, you are the witness of all; therefore, you are hidden within all beings;
therefore, you are the sovereign of all and the one to be worshipped by all—you are the Reality.
Then there is the pair of Śrutis, the eternal Saccidānandā, and further,
the foot consisting of the quality of sattva, together with its expansion.
Following that is the vision of equality, then the two scriptural declarations "That art thou" (*tattvamasi*);
thereafter is the absolute state, which is the very form of liberation and transcends all conceptual construction.
Pervading time yet devoid of that subsequent time, you are likewise supreme;
thus you are perceived as the non-dual Yuga.
92b) Therefore it is beyond the sphere of the senses; therefore it is non-dual; therefore it is indivisible bliss;
therefore it is without cause—"That thou art"—O Great Sage, such is the pair of Vedic statements.
From that arises the existence of temporal relations;
beyond that is the immutable state, free from all mental construction, which is then pure conceptualization.
Devoid [of attributes], transcending causes, likewise inseparable from action, it is to be known through pure experience; that is the reality beyond this.
O Sage, the two Vedic statements "the stainless, pure intellect" and "eternal, true, and liberated by nature" refer to that Supreme. Beyond that is nothing further.
Each is composed of consciousness and subject to modification and transformation;
it is void, free from the veils and distractions, and devoid of all powers.
The state free from delusion is liberated from sorrow, hatred, and ignorance;
the two Vedic statements "That art thou" have that as their ultimate goal: eternal knowledge and will.
The two Vedic statements "I am the agent of great manifestation" and "I am indeed the state of cessation" are complete with dispassion and sovereignty; they are the "That art thou."
The very state of the latent impressions of the intellect, ego,
and mind, devoid of the natural flow of the womb-mind and intellect— that is "Thou art That."

The two-fold scripture is the means of valid cognition and that which is to be cognized; for from that very source arises existence, which is ultimately subtle, beyond the reach of words that serve as the causes for appearances.
The causal relationship is indeed "That thou art," and beyond that is the pair of scriptural statements,
"Being" and "Non-being," which culminates in ultimate tranquility.
Therefore, the two scriptural passages— "That thou art" and "The one without qualities"— serve as witnesses for the purpose of awakening memory and for the sake of [realizing] the ultimate reality.

93a) Thereafter, that which is expressed by the word "Brahman" (vrahma-vācaka-śabda-vācya); thereafter, the pair consisting of the reality (tattva) and its measure (mitāra); and thereafter, the state of the signified and the signifier (vācyavācakapada).
Then follows "Bhāvasiddha Śivaśakti Samaya," and after that,
"Rahasyasaṃpradāyinī," and after that, "Tattvamasi."
The two-fold scripture consists of Nirvāṇa, Kaivalya, Amṛta, Mukti, Niḥśreyasa, Apavarga, and Mokṣa; it is devoted to that [ultimate goal].
Sāmarasya (identity), ekatā (oneness), pratyak (the inward-facing), āpadam (the goal), and nandānubhavatādātmya (identity with the experience of bliss) are therefore synonyms for that state.
Then follow Padadāyinī, the pair of Vedic texts "tat tvam asi," and likewise the supreme;
then Vāṇī, Śruti, Caṭīsiddhi, Bhūḥ, and Retas, which bestow happiness.
Prāntara, Dogdhrī, Śoṣiṇī, Prabaṃdhā,
Dolā, Aṅkuśā, Śivā, Ḍākinī, and Tālī.
*Nihrādinī* and *daṇḍa*, followed by *sakalapadāt*; then *yaṃtramātar*, *jagajjanani*, and thereafter *paramapadam*.
Then, [meditate on] the Compassionate One, whose mind is a tree of mercy, who brings benefit to all; then, [meditate on] the state of birth and death.
Therefore, it consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and sustains the ocean of *saṃsāra*;
furthermore, it is the very state that produces the two-fold form.
Then, for the sake of illuminating each respective state, there is the singing of their respective names;
you are the ground of the yoga of speech, Oṃ, you are beyond the sphere of objects, and you are that which is supreme.
O Caṭī, you are free from conceptual construction; you are the ground of accomplishment, the state of Śambhu, and the supreme station.
Klīṃ! You are the Fourth (Turyā), the bestower of bliss, and you are Nirvāṇa beyond that.
Immediately after that, you shall become Prāntarāpunaḥpadā;
thereafter, you shall be Dogdhrī, Tālaviṃdu, and Śoṣiṇī.
You are the Supreme Self, the eternal bond, and the ever-arisen state;
you are unbroken supreme bliss and the very seed of the swing.
You are of the nature of immediate consciousness; beyond that, you are the seed-syllable of the Sage (Muṇi).
Therefore, from that state of changelessness, you are the stainless one (Nirañjanā) who transcends even that.
O Ḍākinī, you are the eternal truth that purifies the channels;
you transcend the three times and are indeed the seed-syllable TĀLĪ.
You are non-different from the Self and the Supreme Self; you are the seed-syllable of the thundering [Vidyā];
you are the experience beyond all discursive thought; salutations to you, O daughter of the Lotus-born!

Then you are the nectar of liberation (*kaivalya*), the very state of having form (*sākāra*), the bestower of the perfection of enjoyment (*bhoga-siddhi*) and heaven; you are the peak syllable (*kūṭa*) known as Light (*bhāsā*).
Devoid of time, endowed with color, and facing the state of emission;
then follows the peak-syllable named Bhāsā, which is the supreme [state] at the beginning of creation.
Then you should form the *kūṭa* of *kāryasi*; thereafter, you should form the *vārāhika* *kūṭa*.
Then, you should again form that very same *kūṭa* as *bhauktikasargakāryasi*.
Listen, O bull among sages, to that which is joined with time yet devoid of color:
"tiryaksarganisarga" and likewise "karyasipadam."
Then you perform the Vārāhika-kūṭa, which effects protection;
thereafter, you perform the Prabhātika-kūṭa, which effects withdrawal.
Immediately after Karyasitadana, one should establish Rṣikūṭa;
then follows Parākūṭa, and thereafter Jīva and Viśeṣaka.
If you perform the *saṃsthāna* rite, then that very [mantra] is deficient;
if you perform the *maryādā* rite, then it has the seed-syllable of Śānta situated within the letter *ra*.
O best of sages, the Candra-kūṭa is supreme as the union of entities;
though it is devoid of qualities, it is the creator of qualities, and it is to be worshipped as possessing qualities—this is the highest truth.
Formless and indivisible, she is indeed the triad of Śivas;
she is the Yoginī of all accomplishments and the triple peak—listen to what follows that.
Then one should utter the three Vedic branches, which are the state of the Mother of all Siddhis;
thereafter, one should utter the triad: Nityoditā (Ever-Arisen), Nandananditā (Rejoiced by Joy), and Dogdhrī (the Milker).
Immediately after that is the leader of the entire circle of families;
and then, O Goddess Caṇḍakāpālinī, the three goads.
O Brahmin, thereafter there is a triad of *prabandhas* for the *paramahaṃsinīs*,
as well as *nirvāṇamārgadā* and the triad of *śoṣiṇīs*.
Then follows the verse for pacifying the heat of the calamities of uneven [fortune],
and thereafter the three-fold swing for all evils and misfortunes.
Then there is the destroyer of afflictions and the bestower of strength; after that, the triad;
and then the three grounds of accomplishment which carry one across the ocean of all calamities.
Then [the mantra] "sakalaśatrupramathinī," then "tataḥ param," then "retastrayam," and then "nararudhirāṃtravaśāṃbhakṣaṇī."
Then there is the word "sakalā," followed by the three who bestow happiness;
likewise, there are the three female friends who fulfill one's desires.
Then one should say "paramakāruṇikā," followed by "tato mahābhairave," and then "rūpadhāriṇī," and from that point, "nirhrādinī."
She is saluted by the best of the thirty gods, the mother of all mantras,
the embodiment of the threefold speech, affectionate toward those who bow before her, and the destroyer of time.
O Brahmin, Amarā, Tritayā, and Sadāmṛtadhārā— these three,
as well as Varṣiṇī and Prasannānanā, should recite the Trikṣapaṇa mantra.
From the word *nigama-āgama*, one should utter the word *kulākula*;
thereafter, the word *cakrasamaya* follows as that which sets [the teaching] in motion.
Then, likewise, there is Mahākāntāravāsapriyā,
and Mālūratritaya, followed by Dāridryapada.
Then, O Lord of Sages, [there arose] the one who removes the evil destinies of the wicked,
and thereafter the one who destroys the despair of the Daityas who bow before her.
One should remember the three names beginning with "nāmyā," followed by the words "naramuṇḍakīkasa," then "mālābharaṇa," and after that, "taḍiddurga."
Then Piṅgalā with her mass of great matted hair, and after that Carcitā; then the three Nāndīs, and then Koṭi-ulkāmukha.
Surrounded by her attendants, she moves about with pure conduct;
beyond that is the triad of fires blazing like ten million cosmic conflagrations.
Then follows she whose belly is the tongue of a mass of great flames issuing from her mouth,
and who is sparkling with side-glances darting from the corners of her eyes.

And in the three aspects [of the body], there is the broad and thick-limbed form; then [she is] Lambodarī (the pot-bellied one), Gambhīrā (the deep one), and Vṛttanābhipuṇḍarīkā (the one with a rounded lotus-like navel).
One should visualize her as the devourer of timely death, the slayer of Yamāntaka,
with three rolling eyes and a mass of blazing radiance.
Then, from the south, there arose the sound of one dwelling in the most terrifying cremation ground,
followed by the cries of elephants, jackals, and lions, and then the shrieks of *bhāruṇḍa* birds.
"Duṣṭanigrāhiṇī," "iti danujanikṛntinī," the triad beginning with "jaraṇīnām," and "yāvadekasattva."
Then there is Jātisaṃmohinī, followed by Kṣīrasāgarāpadā,
and immediately after that, Chāchamahārudrotsaṅgavāsinī.
And Mahāmāṃsāśinī, as well as the three peaks of Dharā;
likewise Brahmāṇī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
O great sage, there are Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, and likewise Indrī;
as well as Cāmuṇḍā, Śivadūtī, and Caṇḍayogeśvarī.
Mahākāpālinī and Kāmamukhī after that;
then Yamaghaṇṭā and Karālī, and after that Mahāyoginī.
O Lord of Sages, there are the Vāruṇī, the Vāyavyā, and the Āgneyī,
and immediately thereafter the Aiśānī, which causes great terror.
Then follows the dancer upon the stage of the time of the great dissolution;
thereafter, the three great peaks and the word consisting of the syllables *hūṃ hūṃ*.
Then [there was] Ghorarāviṇī, then Narasārddhapada,
and immediately after that, Vigrahā, whose entire body is covered with skin.
Then, O Brahmin, having joined the joints [of the mantra], one should recite "lelihānarasanā," followed by "karālānanā," and then "sarvāyudhā."
Then follow Dhāriṇī, Kukkuṭa, Gṛdhra, Kāka, Ulūka, and Chatrā;
this is the triad of the Rāthantara hymns, a peak with a slight distinction.
O Brahmin Nārada, you know that in its place is the first letter of the class;
after that is Mahāḍāmarī, and Phetkāriṇī follows thereafter.
Then [the mantra] "having the form of a serpent of white, blue, yellow,
and red color," then "adorned with ornaments of coils," and after that "the body."
Then the word *anantakoṭinetra*, followed by the word *kara*,
then *caraṇā*, and then the three words for those who are peaceful (*śānta*).
The syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m* at the end;
she who is fashioned from these, she who moves within the house, and she who is the great void (*mahāgagana*).
Then she is mounted upon a lion-throne, holding a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) in her hand;
thereafter she is adorned with a garland of skeletons and possesses a terrifying smile.
Mahāpāśupata, Trayakūṭa, and Pīvarī; then Dhīvarī, Ḍākinī, Śākinī, and the station of Yoginī.
Then Bhoginī, O son of Brahmā, followed by Kāmonmādinī;
then Duritadiṣṭhotsādinī, and thereafter the three peaks of Nāndī.
Jaṃbhinī, Sthaṃbhinī, Mohinī, and likewise Dohinī;
Nāyikā, Gāyikā, Padāta, Tapinī, and the station of Tāpinī.
Karālī and Vikarālī, and after that Āveśinī;
then Praveśinī, Dhariṇī, and they know Dhāriṇī to follow after that.
96a) Then Śaṅku, then those three from the station of Sarvabhūta; then Damanī, Mahādaṃṣṭrā, and Karālā thereafter.
She is the companion of the Night of Doom (Kālarātri), she is known as the ten-million-fold sun,
she possesses a radiance equal to a [celestial] orb, and she is the dissolution itself.
Having formed the *saṃdhi*, there is the *agnipada* and then the *dussahapada*;
thereafter, the entire body is adorned with the manifestation of touch.
From Trailokyoddāmarī, then Śivahṛdambuja;
thereafter Bhramarī, Śvetavārāhī, and Raktacāmuṇḍā.
Then there is Āpatrayā, Hetutrayā, Sarvavidyeśvarī,
Śvetasarasvatī, Śrutitrayā, and then Caṭī.
Then the *dogdhrī* mantra, encapsulated by the *tāra*, which is the crest-jewel of the Vedas;
then the *dolā* mantra, likewise encapsulated by the *tāra*; and after that, the seed-syllable of the goad (*sṛṇi*).
The syllable *dhāṃ* is encased by the *dhāraṇa* (the letter *ha*), and *hara* (*ha*) is likewise joined with the *bindu*.
Then follow *jagajjanani* and, after that, *jagadāśraye*.

From the word *jagadrūpe* (O you whose form is the universe), [the syllable] *pa*; from the word *jagat* (universe), [the syllable] *li*; from the word *pālinī* (protector), [the syllable] *nī*; from the word *jagatsaṃhāriṇi* (destroyer of the universe), [the syllable] *sa*; and from the word *jagadvandyā* (worshipped by the universe), [the syllable] *va*—thus the *caṭī* mantra is revealed in the Vedas.
The three *caṭīs*, the *samīhā*, the *vaṭī*, and after that the *śoṣiṇī*;
then the *śivādolā* enclosed by a *caṭī*, and likewise the *sṛṇi*.
O Lord of Sages, [the mantra] is written on a birch bark scroll, rubbed clean, and devoid of the *bindu*;
having remembered the placement (*nyāsa*) with two *bindus*, one should recite the word of address, "O Durgā."
Then [the name] Durgadaityamardini, followed by Durgottāriṇī;
then Durgaprabhañjinī, and after that Durgatināśinī.

96b) [The syllable] *caṭī* is known as the accomplisher of difficult deeds, compassionate toward those in miserable states, and the milch-cow; they know these three to be the *tāra* enclosed by the milch-cow.
Then follow the veins Śoṣiṇī and Dogdhrī;
after those, Dolā-dogdhrī, Sṛṇi-dogdhrī, Dhānta-dogdhrī, and likewise Vyāla.
Then, for one who observes the vow of Kaula conduct, he shall bestow the path of the Kula;
thereafter, O crusher of the Kula, he shall set it in motion from the three steps.
Then, after the one who bestows the status of a Kaulika;
then, after that, the Mistress of the Wheel of Kula and Akula.
Then, O Sage, from the word *kulavastu* comes the word *saṃtoṣiṇī*;
[then] *kuladveṣivināśini*, *śoṣiṇī*, and the Veda (*śruti*) encapsulated [by these].
The seed-syllable of Caṭī, Śoṣiṇī, Puṭitā, and Samīhā;
then two Śoṣiṇīs, Śirā, Śoṣiṇī, and Dolakā.
Śoṣiṇī, Aṅkuśaśoṣiṇī, Dhānta, Śoṣiṇī likewise,
Kalānvita, Vyāpana, and Vedamārgaprakāśinī.
Then, having meditated upon the word "Vedana-matra-pada" (the state of mere consciousness), which is to be known through the Vedas and Vedanta,
one should contemplate the supreme word "Hāriṇī-pada" (the Seizer) from its constituent syllables.
Immediately after that, [he saw him] whose majesty was being sung by the Vedas;
then, after that, [him] mounted upon Rudra who consists of the Vedas.
From the word "pratipādyā" [comes] the Vedas; from that, the word "phalapradaṃ" which bestows the fruit of action;
then the word "dātri"; and again the word "śiraḥ," which is the revelation (śruti).
Caṭī, Śirādogdhrī, Śirāśoṣiṇī of the head, the two vessels (śirā) Dolāvīja, Śirāṅkuśa, and also Śirā. 97a)
O Yogīśvarī, [the mantra] ending with *dhāṃ*, joined with the fifth vowel (*ū*) and two dots (*bindu*),
has made its abode in the lotus-heart of the practitioners of yoga.
Then [there is the form] consisting of the body of yoga and illuminating yoga;
thereafter, that which brings about both union with and separation from yoga.
From the channel that bestows yoga, there is then the station where [the breath] is established;
likewise, there are the two ears of the swing, which destroy the bonds of worldly existence through the gift of yoga.
O Sage, [the seed-mantras] are Dolācaṭī, Dolādogdhrī, and likewise Dolāśoṣiṇī;
then the vein (śirā) conjoined with Dolā, and likewise the Sṛṇi-seed.
The syllable *dhāṃ* is encircled by the *dolā* (the vowel *u*), and likewise the fifth [vowel *u*] is joined with *pa*.
Following that is the vocative phrase: "O you who move in the supreme, ultimate void."
Beyond that is the circle of the most fierce staff-like arms;
beyond that is the one who illuminates the supreme state; and beyond that is the Supreme.
Then follows the sequence of words consisting of the supreme, the lower-supreme, and the supreme mantras;
thereafter, that which consists of the body of initiation, yoga, and knowledge.
Then there is the state whose form is primordial nature (prakṛti), like that of the Supreme Person;
then the state which is the transformation of supreme bliss and consciousness.
In the word *rūṣita*, there is a stage of incessant peril;
the invocation is said to be *tāriṇī* (the Savior), and likewise *śruti-sṛṇi* and *śruti-sṛṇi*.
Caṭī, Sṛṇisamīhā, Sṛṇi, and likewise Śoṣiṇī;
Sṛṇi, Śira-aṅkuśa, Dolā, and the three Aṅkuśas as well.
One should utter the word "namaḥ" first, followed by fourteen words;
then from the word "bhuvaneśvari," O Brahmin, one should say "caturvargaphala."
She is the bestower [of boons], known as the eighty-four crores of Brahmāṇḍas;
thereafter follows the state of action consisting of the forms of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Beyond that is the triad which generates the *saṃskāra*,
and from that follows the state consisting of the four-faced, four-armed, and four-formed [deities], and so forth.
And from that, the state of having feet served by hosts of gods;
and from the state of the lotus-feet, the state of the fourfold social order.
Then, O Nārada, [he spoke] on the subject of the conduct prescribed for the four stages of life (āśrama), followed by the subjects of vows, sacrifices, dharma, and fire-offerings (homa).
Then one should utter the invocation dear to the restraints and observances,
as well as the four-limbed verses even during the performance of battle rites.
To Priyā Mahābhairavī and Sahakarmacāriṇī;
then the phrase "encircled by the garland of the four oceans."
Then, one should say "Homage to her who dwells upon the circle of the earth, the abode of all living beings;
homage to the presiding deity of the heart; homage to Pratyaṅgirā."
Then follows the word for action, known as the individual essence of each manifestation;
after that, O Brahmin, the word "namas" (salutation) is prescribed as the impelling term.
Salutations to the word "namaḥ" which removes the misfortunes of all who bow down;
thereafter, salutations to the wisdom of the reflected power of Māyā.
After that, the word "namaḥ" [is placed] for the yantra and mantra honored in each limb;
then again, the word "namaḥ" for the devotee who has been inspired by intuitive insight.
Then, [one should utter] that which removes the fruits of fixed destiny;
then, having uttered the nine-syllable [mantra], and then the word "Navākṣarī."
Then, in the vital breath whose form is the Veda and which pervades the entire body, one should place the syllable *caṭī* on the head; after that, the seed-syllable *dogdhī*.

O Nārada, [the mantra consists of] "to the one whose heart is form" (rūpahṛdāya), then "the drier" (śoṣiṇī) and "the state of carrying form" (rūpavāhapadam); then, starting from the words for the back and the belly, there is the seed-syllable of the companion (sakhīvījam).
Next, the seed-syllable *sṛ* is considered to be placed in the form of the side, waist, thighs, and hips;
thereafter, in the form of a swing, it is in the shanks and feet.
First is the word for form (*rūpa*), then the vocative case for hand, foot, limb, and fingernail; then the word "namas" (homage), then the vocative case for all limbs (*sarvāṅga*).
The state of Nārāyaṇa is attained through the syllable *om*, consisting of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*;
from that arises Hiraṇyagarbha, and thereafter the form of Sadāśiva.
Then, with the syllables *ha*, *ra*, and *ka*, followed by that [vowel],
and likewise the word *hūṃ* which has the form of space (*vyoma*), fire (*agni*), and the letter *ma*.
By the syllable *ha* and *o*, she takes the form of one possessed by wrath;
then, by the syllable *ha* and *ā*, there is the state of the five elements, beginning with *hā*.
Following that is the syllable *vaṃ* in the form of a bond, and then the word *phreṃ*;
thereafter is the word for the four aims of life (*caturvarga*) by means of the letters *pha*, *ra*, and *e*.
She is the embodiment of knowledge and power, and her very word is "kṣaum.
She is composed of the letters *ka* and *ṣa*, and through the letter *kā*, she is the one who effects creation and protection.
The word *tadanukrama* is of the nature of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*);
then, by means of the letters *ka*, *ra*, and *u*, follows the word *janmajarā*.
Then follows the form that causes death and destruction, "namaḥ";
after that, the word formed by the syllables *na*, *ma*, and the *visarga*.
Indeed, the state of the gods, mantras, oblations, food, vital breath, and lifespan is itself the form of Time; there is nothing else beyond that which is not subject to its reversal.
Then, having joined the words for the Brahmāstra, the Vaiṣṇavāstra, and the Pāśupatāstra,
one should join the word for the Āgneyāstra and then the word for the Vāruṇāstra.
Then follows the holder of the Yāmya-weapon, the Gāruḍa-weapon, and the Saṃhāra-weapon;
and likewise the Padam in both direct (anuloma) and reverse (pratiloma) order.
There are thirty-three crores of the forms of the gods; from that, eighteen are the forms of the Vidyās; nine are the forms of the treasures, and [the remainder] is the state of the eight siddhis.
From the category of form (*rūpa*) come the forms of the five elements; hear what follows that:
they are of the singular nature of Brahman, being both the first and the second category.
O Sage, listen: the third is Lajjā, the fourth is Roṣa;
the fifth is Śākinī, and the sixth is the station of Dhāraṇā.
Then follows the phrase "the seventh, the bolt, and the eight prostrations," and thereafter the phrase "tendency toward delusion, birth, old age, and death."
It delivers one from dwelling in the womb, from the three torments, and from saṃsāra.
From the word "sasaṃkitaḥ," one should utter the savior (tāra) and the two bindus.
Evil deeds, seizing the property of others, violence, slander, falsehood, and disputes— these lead to a state of shame away from dharma.
Thus, from shame arise pride, the state of making sounds,
contempt, revilement, joy, and likewise envy.
That which incites one toward wretchedness and hatred is *roṣa*, and it is a Vedic term;
whereas righteousness, conduct, sacrifice, austerity, mantra, and ritual consecration are its highest state.
Beyond that is the stage of meditation (dhyāna), which leads from merits;
then follow the stages of experience (anubhava), contemplation (upāsanā), and the stage of discipline (niyama).
99a) Because she is able [to bestow] supreme knowledge, dispassion, and the very state of dharma and artha through her certainties, she is therefore called Śākinī thereafter.

Then [the feet] of those who move on the earth, those who move in the air, and those who move within; then likewise the feet of those who move in water, those who dwell in houses, and those who move in their limbs.
Therefore, it is called *dhāraṇā* because it sustains [the mind] from that which moves and that which is unmoving;
it is the state beyond false scriptures, wrong words, and the sphere of erroneous doctrines and improper conduct.
It wards off bad disciples, the state of following wrong paths, and the state of evil intellect from bad conduct and bad methods;
therefore, it is called an "argalā" (a bolt).
Then there is the stage of bowing down and rising up,
as well as the stage of counteracting, distress, and despair.
Therefore, because it brings about the cessation of obstacles and leads [the soul] toward [liberation],
"praṇāma" is the essence of all the Vedas and Agamas, as well as the Śruti.
Caṭī, Dogdhrī, Śoṣiṇī, as well as Śivā, Dolā, and Aṅkuśā—
these should be worshipped with the supreme name "Namaḥ" (Salutation).
Then there is Trisatya, Śruticaṭyo, and the word Dogdhrī;
likewise, in the Satya Yuga, there are Śoṣiṇī and Śivādolā.
Thus, in the Tretā Yuga, there was "Kroṃ" followed by the word "Namaḥ";
and in the Dvāpara Yuga, there was "Śruticaṭī" followed by "Krodhāḥ."
Then there are Śoṣiṇī, Śivādolā, and Sṛṇidaṇḍā; following that, in the Kali Yuga, this very state [arises].
Thereafter, by those who know all the *Nigamas* and *Āgamas*, that supreme state was synthesized and practiced; then the seeker of liberation [attained] that very state.
